paragraphs.text: The rays illuminate the children of light, and the messages of light make them radiant. The light of those who worship God is their devotion to God, which dispels the haze and fog of ignorance. The light of truth dawns upon those who love learning. Just as this visible light illuminates the body, so truth illuminates the soul. And just as by day we distinguish from one another the sick and the healthy, the beautiful and the ugly, the low and the high, the smooth and the rough, the road and the wrong path, the thorn and the vine shoot, the mud and the springs; and at night, all appearances [?]. So too, brothers, when truth dawns, it hides ignorance and reveals the health of faith and the sickness of unbelief, the beauty of humility and the ugliness of licentiousness, the baseness of arrogance and the smoothness of uprightness, the willfulness of wickedness, the vine shoots of virtue and the thorns of sins, the mud of desire and the springs of righteousness.

For this very reason, blessed David sings of light and truth together in one refrain, saying, “Send out your light and your truth.” What light and truth does he wish to send? It is clearly that light of which John says, “He was the true light, which enlightens every person who is to come into the world.” For our Lord Jesus Christ is the true light, the ray of devotion to God, the Sun of righteousness, the Dawn of truth, who rises from on high and gives light from the earth. From on high he shines in glory according to his divinity, and from the earth he rises upward according to the dispensation of his flesh. The Dawn, which is the intelligible light, rises from on high, according to blessed Zechariah, the father of John the Forerunner, who says, “Through this, the Dawn from on high has visited us.” That same Dawn rises again from the earth. Of him, the other Zechariah, his namesake among the twelve prophets, says, “Behold a man, and his name is Dawn.”

And from where does he rise? David explains: “Truth sprang up from the earth.” What truth? Do not learn from me, but directly from the giver of life to all. “I am,” he says, “the way and the truth and the life.” As was already said earlier in the first discourse, he is a simple and expansive nature, indivisible, incorporeal, and without form, just like his Father who begot him. And he takes upon himself various names because of his beneficence. He is called the way in order to drive away wandering; and truth, in order to destroy falsehood; and life, in order to undo death.

And see how often he assumes names that seem contrary in wording but agree in their effect. The same one is a shepherd; the same one is a sheep. “I am,” he says, “the good shepherd.” And how is he a sheep? John says, “Behold the Lamb of God.” And [?] those who wish to introduce distinctions through different names say, “How can being a sheep and being a shepherd be one nature?” Is Christ’s nature to be divided by these various names? It is clearly evident that the various names signify not his essence but his activity. He calls himself a shepherd and is also named a sheep. He is called a priest and is also designated a priest’s temple. As it says, “You are a priest according to the order of Melchizedek”; and a temple, as it says, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”

Let every error be uprooted, and let truth reign, prevail, and rule over everyone. And our Lord Jesus Christ called himself the vine, as he was, and as we brought out in the discourse, and called the Father the gardener, not introducing any change in his nature, but describing the renewal brought about by his saving work. For everything given to the people of old was ruined. The priesthood was given, and it became corrupt; kingship was given, and prophecy was given. Israel became a [?] vine, as the prophet Jeremiah also says, and instead of the fruit of worshiping God, it produced injustice. Likewise Isaiah also says, “I waited expectantly for grapes, and it produced thorns.” And because he saw everything ruined and grown old through negligence, he came and personally renewed everything. He becomes everything to everyone, not himself being divided, but putting everything in order according to a single plan.

And the Scriptures testify that all these things were ruined and corrupted among the Jews: “Their priests,” he says, “did not say, ‘Where is the Lord?’” “And their prophets practiced divination for silver, and their messengers did not know me, and their rulers dishonored me, and my people did not know me.” And because everything, including the ordinances of worshiping God, had been ruined, he came and personally restored the priesthood, established kingship, renewed prophecy, and through his gifts of grace renewed everything that had been ruined and corrupted. The priesthood was ruined, and he himself became a priest. Of him the apostle says, “We have such a high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the Majesty in the heights.” And because the kingship of the Jews had been taken away, the King of the saints came and entered. Of him Nathanael says, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel.” And because false prophecies had obscured prophecy, God took away the gift of prophecy because the inhabitants of the land were unworthy. He came personally to renew prophecy once again, as the blessed Moses also said: “The Lord God will raise up a prophet for you.”

Thus he was a prophet, a priest, and a king—not because he himself needed that honor, but to raise up those who had fallen. For the King of kings had no need of kingship; nor was he lacking in priesthood, since he received service from every priesthood. Nor did he need prophecy, since he was the fountain of prophecy and poured out streams of righteousness through all the prophets. Rather, he came to raise up everything that had fallen, and to restore and renew everything that had been ruined. He also found the vine of Israel corrupted, of which David says, “The vine that you brought out of the land of the Egyptians—you uprooted the nations and planted it.” And, renewing what had been corrupted, he says, “I am the true vine.” Not that he is by nature something to be cultivated, but through grace he renews what has been corrupted. If the vine is something to be cultivated, how can he sow like a gardener tending a vine? Speaking about his own teaching, he says, “Look, the sower went out to sow.” And he himself explains who the sower is: “The one who sows the seed,” he says, “is the Son of Man.” How, then, can one and the same person be both something cultivated and a cultivator, a sower of seeds? Unless you distinguish them and attribute the one to his divinity and the other to his saving work in the flesh, you confuse these things with one another and will not understand the truth. He says, “I am the vine,” and calls himself the vine’s cultivator, just as elsewhere he calls himself both shepherd and sheep. And from this very point the heretics perversely interpret what was rightly written, just as the prophet says, “The ways of the Lord are straight, and the righteous will walk in them.” They do not understand what is correct, or what is clarified and distinguished through the proper ordering of the mind: to assign one half to the honor of his divinity and the other half to his incarnate dispensation. For this reason they mixed everything together and corrupted it, and filled the whole world with the fog of error.

For the Savior and Lord, who loves humanity, came into this world for our sake, without departing from the honor he possessed before the ages. Rather, in his love for humanity he made provision for us and revealed the two radiant expressions of the truth: [?] through signs, and his humanity through sufferings. For the one incapable of suffering entered into suffering through what was capable of suffering—not through those passions that lead to sins, but through those that encompass our common nature. For body and soul are subject to passions that lead to sins, and whoever is free of those passions is also free of sins. It is like this: hunger, thirst, weariness, and sleep are bodily needs, but they are not counted as sins. But sexual immorality, impurity, and debauchery, which defile the beauty of the body, are sinful passions. The soul, too, has passions surrounding it, received by nature from the Creator and necessary for salvation: fear, sorrow, and anger. If examined individually, they are called passions, but in moderation and at the proper time they assist our nature.

And pay attention: there is righteous anger, and wrath called righteous—not anger that flares up without cause, but anger stirred by divine righteousness, often through the influence of the Holy Spirit. It is not when someone becomes angry without cause, but when someone is enraged for the sake of the worship of God. Scripture bears witness: “The Spirit of the Lord came upon Saul,” it says, “and he became angry.” When righteous anger is put to use for righteous deeds, Scripture praises it. When it is kindled against impiety, when it serves to silence heretics, when the battle is for the glory of the great King, then showing anger is good, and concealing it is treachery. Pay attention, brother, also to desire—not the desire that falls into sins, but the desire that adorns our race through lawful marriage. Pay attention to fear—not fear that is vain, but fear that is useful and beneficial. For where there is fear of God, there are gifts of goodness, and where there are fears arising from impiety, there are futile deeds. I speak of fear: our giver of life took upon himself the passions of body and soul that are apart from sins. In his body he hungered, thirsted, grew weary, and slept. By this he did not dishonor his divinity in any way, but truly revealed the nature of his body. Likewise, in his soul he feared, was distressed, and grieved. “My soul,” he says, “is sorrowful to the point of death.” And again, he began to grieve and be distressed. These were not sinful passions, but indications of the nature of his body.

And to make it still clearer that such words do not apply to his divinity but to his body, the giver of life explains to the disciples what kind of passions these are: “My soul,” he says, “is sorrowful to the point of death. Stay awake, so that you do not enter into temptation.” And immediately there he says, “The spirit is willing, but the body is weak.” And thus, in every way, he truly demonstrates the honor of his divinity and the dispensation of his flesh. He ate as a human being; he fed others as one who loves humanity. And what is still more astonishing is that, while he was asking for a drink, he gave the whole world drink. He says to the Samaritan woman, “Give me a drink.” And he raises his voice and says, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink.” He sleeps on the sea to confirm the reality of his bodily nature, and, rising, he puts the waves of the sea to sleep, so that you may learn that he both sleeps and puts others to sleep. As God, he knows beforehand everything that was happening everywhere, and as a human being, he traveled through the regions of Galilee. And coming to stand opposite Bethany, Lazarus’s village, he shows himself both far away and near through the distance between the places [?]. And by the power of his divinity he knows everything beforehand. In Galilee he recounts the things that were happening in Judea. “Lazarus, our friend,” he says, “has fallen asleep.” And though he was not nearby, he was at work in that place. Coming, he stands by the village and says, “Where have you laid him?” And who would dare bring an accusation of ignorance against Christ because he asked, “Where have you laid him?” And if these words cause you to stumble, [?], for words like these are also spoken of Christ’s Father. Is the Father’s saying, “Where are you, Adam?” also an expression of ignorance? This utterance is a counterpart to that utterance. Christ asks, “Where have you laid him?” And God also asks in the Old Testament, “Where is Abel your brother?”

But perhaps someone will say, “That does not resolve the mystery, but adds to the difficulties, for you have shown that not only Christ asks questions, but Christ’s Father does too.” If that is so, let the meaning of both the Father’s and the Son’s questions also be explained. First learn the meaning of the one who asked there, and of this one here. But when I say “that one there” and “this one here,” I do not mean that the one is someone different, or that the other is someone different. Rather, whatever is said in the Gospel I refer to the Father, and whatever is said in the Old Testament I attribute to the Son. For nothing, either in the new writings or in the old, happened without Christ’s power. As John also testifies, not only concerning creation but concerning the entire dispensation: “Everything,” he says, “came into being through him, and without him nothing came into being that came into being.” And learn what the meaning of his question to Cain, “Where is Abel your brother?” was: by asking, he opened for him a way to give an answer. He judges as a righteous judge, and calls to repentance as one who loves humanity. “Where,” he says, “is Abel your brother?” As a judge, he brings him before the tribunal. And Cain, taking the question as evidence of his ignorance, wanted to hide the matter from his benefactor. “I do not know,” he says. “Was I my brother’s keeper?” And what follows? Consider the intention. The one who knows everything explains to him: “I deliberately pretended ignorance, but you supposed that I was asking without knowing anything.” “If that is so, learn the knowledge of the all-knowing one: the cry of your brother’s blood appeals to me from the earth.”

Now learn also the intention of the benefactor, and what he meant when he said to the Jews, “Where have you laid him?” The crowds of spectators had become ungrateful—a people who could not comprehend these miracles. Or rather, they did understand, but in their ingratitude they wanted to conceal the miracles. He saw them behaving arrogantly and mocking the miracles. He looked at them, because they saw the mighty works and denied the wonder-worker [?], as David also testifies: “Because of your great power, your enemies lied to you.” And what would he do about this? He could have gone silently. Indeed, he need not even have gone bodily, but could have sent his power, and with the rays of his power he could have opened the tomb, raised the dead man, and brought into the light the one imprisoned in darkness. But he wants the ungrateful people themselves to be witnesses of the miracles. Before revealing the tomb, he first prompts the many ungrateful people, saying, “Where have you laid him?” “Come,” they say, “and see the tomb.” And he says to them, “Roll away that stone.” You who became the disciples’ guarantor and gave them power as a pledge, saying, “If you have faith like a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move,’ and it will move”— you who granted them immeasurable authority, could you not roll away one small stone at the entrance of the tomb? But, as I said earlier, it was for those same reasons: they were unbelieving judges and disobedient spectators, and they said, “The affair of the dead man must be some deception and illusion; he must be lying there under a pretext, listening for the supposed arrival [?].” Therefore he brings them themselves to the tomb, so that when they roll away the stone and the smell strikes their faces, the dead man’s smell may testify to them that he is truly dead, so that when they believe that the dead man is dead, they will then have no doubts about his resurrection either.

And that he devised such means in his coming down [?], pay attention to the sequence there, and you will learn. Martha approached the stone and said, “Lord, he already smells, for he has been dead four days.” But the giver of life, knowing his power, says, “This is precisely what I want to learn from you. Say it, and say it repeatedly: that he smells. Confirm that he is dead, so that the resurrection too may be proclaimed truthfully.” He repeatedly mentioned death, so that at least once the truth of the resurrection too might be confessed. Then, brothers, the giver of life arranges something else. He looks up to heaven and calls upon the Father. “Father,” he says, “I thank you because you have heard me.” The disciples of the heretics find some remedy in these words and immediately pounce on them. “Do you see,” they say, “how great a difference there is between them? One asks, and the other is asked; one entreats, and the other listens to the entreaties. Do you see that the Father is the source of the miracles and grants the Son the power to perform miracles?” But, as I have said many times before, they did not take care to discern the works of the giver of life with gratitude. Instead, already caught up in blasphemy, they became blind, unable to discern the truth.

But learn the reasons [?] from today’s reading. The giver of life says to them, “I have shown you many good works from my Father. For which of these works do you stone me?” The Jews say to him, “We do not stone you for good works, but for blasphemy, because you are a man and make yourself God, and call God your Father.” This greatly distressed the Jews: that he called God his own Father. The Jews were angry with Christ not only because he broke the Sabbath, but also because he called God his Father and made himself equal to God. And because they treated calling God his Father as blasphemy, he holds court at the tomb and seats truth as the judge. He brings the ungrateful people around him as witnesses, so that they may see with their eyes and hear with their ears—the very people who said, “You blaspheme because you call yourself the Son of God.” He calls him Father, and by this very act he almost instructs them: “Look, I call him this in your very presence. If he becomes angry because I call him Father, and if this is blasphemy, as you think, then let him not hear me.” “But if he does not become angry, then it is clear that he truly is my Father.” “Father,” he says, “I thank you because you have heard me.” If the prayers were an act of obedience, how does he say, before beginning to pray, “You have heard me”? For before beginning to pray, he says, “Father, I thank you because you have heard me.” And he directs the thoughts of those standing around him: “If the Father becomes angry,” he says, “because I call him Father, and this is blasphemy against God, as you think, let him not become an accomplice of me, the blasphemer. But if I call the dead man and he obeys the command, take the deeds themselves as a demonstration of the truth. For raising the dead is not the work of a blasphemer, but the command of the Son of God.” He himself bears witness that this is the meaning of the prayers, and that he made use of prayer not for any need of his own, but for the benefit and correction of his hearers, when he said, “Father, I thank you because you have heard me,” and added, “I already knew that you always hear me, but I said this because of the people standing around me.”

From now on, let no one confuse the truth; let no one oppose the worship of God; let no one reckon his descent for our salvation as weakness or as a dishonor to the Holy One. For your sake, the lover of humanity became human, not casting aside his own nature, but raising up the fallen and bringing the dead to life. He takes what is yours and gives what is his. He did not come to his original honor through his saving work; rather, from his divinity he came to take the saving work upon himself. It is not as the disciples of the heretics suppose, that after the cross and the saving work he advanced in honor. For they impiously wish to patch certain stains onto the apostle’s words, when, speaking of the giver of life, he says, “Who, being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself and took the form of a servant, and, becoming like a human being and being found in appearance as a human being, humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.” And he adds to this: “Therefore God also exalted him still higher and bestowed on him the name that is above every name.” “Do you see,” they say, “that he received honor as the payment for his obedience? For he humbled himself to the point of death, and therefore God also exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name.” If that is so, let them listen. If he received his advancement as a reward for his saving work, then he advanced from poverty to riches. Now pay attention, I beg you. If he received his advancement as a reward for obedience, then he came from poverty to riches, to receive worship from everyone, so that every knee [?] should bow at the name of Jesus Christ. You say that he was poor and came to riches through his saving work. But Paul does not agree with you, for he does not show him coming from poverty to riches, but taking poverty upon himself while possessing riches.

What does the apostle say? “You know, brothers,” he says, “the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: though he was rich, he became poor for our sake, so that you might become rich through his poverty.” So that you might become rich, not so that you might blaspheme. Our Lord Jesus Christ became poor, not casting aside his eternal riches—I mean his divinity—but concealing that and taking this poverty upon himself. What is his greatness? The Father is called rich; the Son too is called rich: rich from the rich. Of him Paul says that God himself enriches all who call upon him, and again, “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” Likewise Jesus is rich, and became poor for our sake. And how is he rich? Because he is of one essence with the Father, the light of his glory, the imprint of his being, and the image of the invisible Father. He did not become such through possessions, but was revealed to be such by nature. Christ’s greatness is this: he is equal to the Father himself, and has the same power, glory, and kingdom, sharing the Father’s throne, with the same honor and the same reverence. But see into what poverty he descended, though he possessed such greatness and sat above with the Father: he stood before Pilate in court like a man condemned to death. Christ’s greatness is the tens of thousands of angels who stand in his service; Christ’s poverty is the twelve fishermen who followed him. Christ’s greatness is his throne in heaven and his sitting at the Father’s right hand; and his poverty is that foxes had dens and the birds of heaven had resting places, but the Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head. Christ’s poverty is his riding on a donkey, and Christ’s greatness is his mounting the cherubim. Of this the prophet says, “The chariots of God are tens of thousands, and thousands are their drivers.” Have you seen his surpassing greatness? Have you seen his poverty, filled with the work of salvation?

But perhaps, stirred up by heretics against the loftiness of this teaching about God, you will say, “Does the statement refer to the giver of life, ‘The chariots of God are tens of thousands’? Does the testimony you have brought apply to him at all? Did it say ‘the chariots of the Son,’ or ‘the chariots of the honor of the Only-Begotten’?” And now, so that devotion to God may not be bartered away by prejudiced listeners, and so that the testimony may not seem irrelevant, it is necessary to demonstrate that “the chariots of God are tens of thousands, and thousands are their drivers” applies to our Lord Jesus Christ. Blessed David says, “The chariots of God are tens of thousands, and thousands are their drivers, and the Lord is among them, at Sinai, in holiness. He ascended on high and led captivity captive, and gave gifts to the children of men.” David says this. Let us call into our midst the interpreter of the prophets, the loud-sounding trumpet, the tongue of the Holy Spirit, the one aflame with power and every grace—Paul, the singer of the Holy One. Let us see to whom he applies the chariots of God and the words, “He ascended on high and led captivity captive, and gave gifts to the children of men.” The apostle says, “One Lord and one faith and one baptism, and one God, the Father of all, through all and in all. But to each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift.” For he indeed says, “He ascended on high, led captivity captive, and gave gifts to the children of men.” And, putting the meaning of Paul’s words to work, he says, “What does ‘he ascended’ mean, except that he first descended into the lower regions of the earth? The one who descended is the same one who ascended into heaven, so that he might fill everything.”

There is no need for many tongues to explain, nor for many words to persuade, but for grateful minds and unity of faith, united in the confession of the Son of God. For he did not say ‘unbegotten and offspring,’ nor ‘uncreated and creature,’ because that is not unity of faith. Listen to Paul, who says, “Until we all come and attain to one unity of faith and knowledge of the Son of God.” Unity of faith is knowledge of the Son of God, not of the unbegotten and the begotten. Why do you snatch away what is written? Is not the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit more trustworthy than “unbegotten” and “begotten,” and what is written more trustworthy than what is not written?

But the heretic counters: “Why, then,” they say, “do you speak of ‘the same essence,’ which is not written?” In the danger of warfare, it is necessary to take up equipment that would be of no use in peacetime. Who put us into the struggles of war? Was it not hostility as vast as the sea? And who would prepare weapons against enemies when peace abounds on every side? First set aside “of a different essence,” so that you are not countered with “of the same essence.” But if you say “of a different essence,” you must be confronted with “of the same essence.” Then, if you remain silent, I too will remain silent, and I recognize the new essence that belongs to the Father as belonging also to the Son. For the names “Father” and “Son” have the same force. For the name of Father and Son is of the same essence: the Father is the Son’s Father, and the Son is the Father’s Son, and the Holy Spirit is God’s Spirit.

But see what the heretics suffer. For they were the first to stir up war, and they are ashamed to set aside such ideas. See what God’s grace does in response to this. He saw them disobeying God’s laws and placed them under the compulsion of Roman laws. For [?] God himself does the same when he sees someone fighting against the laws of worshiping God: he raises up against them God’s [?] of men, because they did not retain the fear of God. See what he does. Anger flares up in the mind of the God-fearing king, and he writes edicts concerning the worship of God through God-fearing servants, and shoots his commands like arrows from the bow of the laws.

The Life-giver likewise often did this to the ungrateful Jews who had refused to worship him. When he spoke the truth, they would say: “By what authority do you do this?” He replies in turn with words that could bring them to fear men: “I too will ask you one question. Where did John’s baptism come from—from heaven or from men?” The Jews reasoned among themselves and said: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he says, ‘Then why did you not believe him?’ But if we say, ‘It was from men,’ we fear the people, lest we be stoned.” And because they had no fear of God, they put the fear of men before themselves: “For fear of men, we dare not say.” And what did the Life-giver do in response? “Neither will I tell you. You do not even know, but I know and will not say.”

And thus God stirred the mind of the God-fearing king. For kingship is righteousness. Pay attention: kingship is also righteousness when it stands in God’s service. Kingship and righteousness stand on the same level. When they are truly servants of the kingdom, they share in God’s honor. And hear what Scripture says: “The souls of the righteous are in God’s hands.” And what does it say of kings? “The king’s heart,” it says, “is in God’s hand.” And why, then, the heart? Because the heart is the source of thoughts and the root of plans; laws come forth from that source. For the words of kings are laws. He holds the heart in his hand so that the laws may not pour forth as though from human thoughts, but may come forth as though from God’s hand. The king establishes laws in agreement with God’s laws. Kingship stands firm to exact vengeance on behalf of the heavenly kingdom. Not because the heavenly kingdom is incapable of taking vengeance on its adversaries, but so that God's grace may open the door of devotion to God for those who are zealous.

And if we investigate carefully, we will find that whenever and wherever impiety waged war, God did not take vengeance without some righteous person. If there is no righteous man standing in between as a mediator, he does not take vengeance on the wicked. Rather, he puts to use a human instrument full of righteousness. Sodom and Gomorrah acted impiously, and all five cities were not destroyed until Lot had settled in the land. So that the inhabitants of the land might not say, 'There was no one to look to, no one's way of life to emulate,' he brings the righteous man to live in Sodom. He lived in the same place, yet was apart from them in his way of life. So that they might find no excuse in their defense, saying that they had no teacher, Lot appeared in Sodom, and vengeance came upon it. For they did not seek to emulate either the example or the righteous man, and they perished in fiery wrath.

Likewise, Pharaoh the Egyptian also fought against God, pleading ignorance. The plagues did not come upon him until Moses appeared to Israel. Ahab, king of the Israelites, also acted impiously; he [?] in lawless impiety. Yet there were no threats of wrath anywhere until the zealous Elijah appeared. Likewise, even now God is able to avenge himself and this church, which is at war. But he raises up fighters for devotion to God, and wishes to care for the church through the [?] of devotion to God. In the same way, blessed Elijah brought an accusation against Israel before God when he entered the wilderness, persecuted by Jezebel. In other words, God says to him, 'Why, Elijah?' God asks him, 'What are you doing here?' He went into that wilderness where Moses received the law, and says, 'I have been very zealous for the Lord God Almighty, because the children of Israel have abandoned you. They have torn down your altars and killed your prophets. I alone remain, and they seek my life.' He says this not as though teaching God, but to bring an accusation; not as though informing someone who is ignorant, but as though presenting a charge to a judge. 'They have torn down your altars and killed your prophets. I alone remain, and they seek my life.'

And because he was provoking God as a judge, and by his accusation stirring him to anger as one who inflicts punishment, God wished to convince the prophet that he bears with the impious out of patience, and does not refrain from punishing them out of weakness. He says to him, 'And behold, tomorrow you will go out before me. And behold, a violent wind will shatter the mountains and grind the hills to dust, but the Lord will not be in the wind. And behold, an earthquake, but the Lord will not be in the earthquake. And behold, fire, but the Lord will not be in the fire.' And what is the meaning of all this? 'Since you think that I cannot exact vengeance, I will convince you that it is not out of weakness that I refrain from bringing punishment upon the sinner. See what means of vengeance I have. What the sword, fire, and casting into the sea accomplish for your judges, these accomplish for me, the great Judge. See what [?] of punishment I have: a violent wind that can shatter not only human beings, but also break mountains and grind hills to dust. Yet the Lord is not in the wind.' This is as much as to say, 'I do not wish to be known for severity, but to be admired for gentleness.' 'Behold, a violent wind,' he says, 'and it shatters the mountains and grinds the hills to dust, but the Lord is not in the wind.' “Here is a mighty wind,” he says, “which shatters the mountains and crushes the hills, but the Lord is not in the wind.” “Here is an earthquake”—instead of saying, “I can also destroy by an earthquake.” And, “Here is fire, but the Lord is not in the fire.” He shows these things, but does not put them into action.

You yourselves bear witness to this from your own experience: he showed an earthquake and made fire flash around the cities; he frightened them but did not punish them. He showed it and held it back. Fire flashed around the cities; the threats arrived, but his love for humanity intervened first. And one could see, he says, the people strengthened and surrounded by a wall of love for humanity. And one could see everyone receiving help from great intercessors, with kingship and priesthood acting as guardians and intercessors. For the God-fearing king joined with the priesthood in intercession and moved God with his entreaties. For a righteous king can accomplish this just as the priesthood that [?] can; and kingship, through intercession, brought God to consent. His glory and upright conduct were revealed through his gentleness. It is clear that he is the son of the great king. For the former stopped the arrows of the barbarians, and the latter, through prayers, dispelled the arrows that rained down from the clouds.

Something like this also happened with the blessed David: God threatens and shows his love for humanity. See what the lover of humanity does: “Here, I give you three blows to choose from. Ask for whichever one you wish: either famine for three years, or war for three months, or death by pestilence for three days.” If you judge as a judge, why give him a choice? Rather, punish him outright, for you have magnified justice. He leaves the decision to him: “Whatever you wish,” he says, “I will do.” Though angry, he promises to listen. But the blessed David, bewildered by the choices, says, “I am hemmed in on every side,” and does not know what to choose: would famine be better, or war, or death? He necessarily accepts death by pestilence for three days—not at random, but so that the king’s devotion to God might become evident. “If I ask for famine,” he says, “I will fall under suspicion of disregarding the destruction of the multitude because I have abundant provisions in my kingdom. And if I ask for war, it is possible to deliver the soldiers to death while keeping myself out of it. I will choose and ask for death, which passes equally among everyone, which shows no favoritism to the rich and no mercy to the lowly, which does not honor rulers or draw back before the poor, so that it may be clear that he offered himself along with everyone else.

“The angel [?] went among them,” he says, “from dawn until the sixth hour, and killed seventy thousand men from among the people.” When God saw that the blows had grown severe and there was no one to entreat him, because the blows were not visible, he allowed David to see the angel holding a sword in his hand and hovering in the air. He offered himself and said, “I, the shepherd, have sinned; what sin have these sheep committed? Let your hand be against me and against my father’s house.”

This saying is akin to the saying in the Gospel: “I am the good shepherd. He lays down his life for his sheep.” When he offered himself, [?] entreated God, who said to the angel, “Return the sword to its sheath.” Humility intervened first: by falling down before God, he won over the great Judge. Just as the king there offered himself and dispelled the anger against everyone, so here too our still more God-fearing king, clothing himself in humility together with everyone— Instead of traveling in chariots and on horseback, he went on foot, and through his gentleness he lessened the punishments. And because he received kindness, he repays his benefactor; and because the kingdom was protected, he strengthens the church. For this very reason God said to Elijah, “Go, anoint Elisha for me as prophet in your place, and Jehu son of Amaziah as king over Israel; and take vengeance on the house of Ahab.” What! Is a man to take vengeance? Rather, this was to show that a God-fearing kingdom avenges the truth. And that is enough on this matter.

From now on, brothers, let us flee the harm caused by heretics and their many waves, and bring the ship into a sheltered and peaceful harbor. Let us hurry, lest God's righteousness arrive and sweep away our sins. For example, if wood, grass, and reeds lie fallen on the ground in a field, while the weather is warm and clear, even though they lie scattered, they do not move from their place; but when a violent flood rises, it carries away the wood, the grass, and the reeds together. Likewise, when God's judgment comes and the great tribunal of Christ is revealed, it sweeps away every error and purges every sin, as the prophet testifies, saying, “Judgment will overflow like water, and righteousness will rush mightily like torrents.”

But let us bring our words to a close here, and call upon the father of us all, the resounding [?], the spiritual instrument. Let us call upon the one hidden and revealed among the treasures of the Egyptians, for those in the church are not to rise against one another as enemies, but to be a refuge for one another. Although their languages differ, one is proclaimed in all languages. Speech does not divide those whom faith does not divide; words do not divide those whom the wise teachers of the church join to one another in unity. Speak of all the practices of the church. Bless the Lord from the springs of Israel. The springs of Israel are the prophetic teachings and the Law; the springs of salvation are the apostles and the gospel of salvation. Come forward, all of you, and draw the water of joy from the springs of salvation.
